title: Mixed Signals, episode 1: a kiss hello in Buenos Aires
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? On a park bench in Buenos Aires, Robin says hello to Flor, and Flor says hello back the Argentine way.

In Argentina, one light kiss on the cheek is the usual greeting, even when you've only just been introduced, and between women and men alike.

Mate, by the way, is the herbal tea Argentines share from a gourd, sipped through a metal straw. Being offered some is friendly, not a proposal.

And at the end? In Bulgaria, a shake of the head means yes.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 2: yes or no in Bulgaria
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? In a village square in Bulgaria, a grandmother offers Robin some banitsa, and Robin would love to join the horo.

In Bulgaria, a shake of the head means yes and a nod means no. Some Bulgarians switch to the other way round for visitors, so when in doubt, listen for да (yes) and не (no).

Banitsa is flaky pastry with white cheese and egg. A horo is a line dance, and newcomers join at the end of the line.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 3: bring a plate in Australia
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? At a backyard barbecue in Australia, the neighbour says "bring a plate", and Robin brings one. An empty one.

In Australia, "bring a plate" means bring a dish of food to share: a salad, a dessert, something for the table. Not the plate. In some places it means bring your own meat for the barbecue, so if in doubt, ask the host what to bring.

A pav is a pavlova, a snag is a sausage, and a barbie is a barbecue.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 4: gursha in Ethiopia
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? At a family's lunch in Addis Ababa, the grandfather holds a mouthful to Robin's lips, and all Robin can see is a baby being spoon fed.

In Ethiopia, gursha is a mouthful of food, wrapped in injera, placed in your mouth by hand: a sign of respect and welcome, and elders and guests get the first. Turning it down is rude. Accept it, and offer one back.

Injera is the soft, sour flatbread the whole meal is eaten with. And the coffee ceremony: green beans roasted over charcoal, incense burning, and coffee poured from a clay jebena, usually in three rounds.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 5: one more cup in Saudi Arabia
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? In a desert tent in Saudi Arabia, Robin is set on being the perfect guest, so the little coffee cup keeps coming back full.

In Saudi Arabia, Arabic coffee is poured from a dallah into tiny cups, a little at a time, elders and guests first, and it keeps coming for as long as you hand your cup back. When you've had enough, give the cup a gentle shake as you hand it over. Take it in your right hand; dates usually come with it.

Tafaddal is a warm "please, go ahead", and alayk bil afya is a Gulf way of saying "to your health" over food and drink.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 6: ftou, ftou, ftou in Greece
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? On a Greek island, a grandmother is charmed by Robin, and every compliment she pays comes with "ftou, ftou, ftou". Robin takes it for being spat at.

In Greece, "ftou, ftou, ftou" is a mock spit, said three times after a compliment, above all to a child or about someone's beauty or health. Nobody really spits: it's only the sound, often with a little turn of the head, to keep the evil eye (the mati) away from someone worth envying. The blue glass eye charm is the best known protection against it. So if you hear it, it's love, not an insult. Smile and say efcharistó.

Κούκλα μου means "my doll", and χρυσό μου "my golden one": both everyday words of affection.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 7: the silent sauna in Finland
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? In a family's lakeside sauna on a winter night in Finland, Robin fills a perfectly comfortable silence with chatter, and takes the quiet for dislike.

In Finland, silence is part of the conversation, and small talk isn't expected. Saunas are usually peaceful and quiet, and a quiet sauna is good company. Löyly is the steam that rises when water is thrown on the hot stones: "Heitä löylyä" asks someone to throw on some more, and "hyvät löylyt", good löyly, is what Finns say after a good sauna. If someone hands you the ladle, you're one of them. Throw a little at a time, and ask the others first.

Mukava tyyppi means "lovely person": what the old man says once Robin has gone.

title: Mixed Signals, episode 8: keep the change in Tokyo
desc:
Better with the sound on.

Ever feel like you're talking two different languages? In a tiny ramen shop in a Tokyo backstreet on a rainy night, Robin wants to say thank you in a big way, leaves the change as a tip, and takes the waiter's chase for trouble.

In Japan, tipping isn't expected, and a waiter may run after you to give back your change. In a small restaurant you pay on the way out, laying the money on the little cash tray. To thank them for the meal, say gochisōsama deshita. And when you walk in, the staff call out irasshaimase, welcome: it needs no reply.

That gold coin with the hole is five yen. Go en sounds like goen, a connection, so lots of people think it lucky.
